chapter.name: Unity in Diversity, or 'Many in the One'

questions.q: Rohan tells his class: 'The People of India project showed that almost every Indian still lives where he or she was born.' Which finding of that same project goes against Rohan's claim?
questions.a: The project observed that many Indians may be called migrants, people not living near their birthplace or with their original community. The other three are true figures from the chapter, but none of them says anything about where people live compared with where they were born.
o: Many Indians are migrants, living away from their birthplace
It counted 325 languages written in 25 different scripts
It surveyed 4,635 communities spread across all the States
India's population is about 18 percent of the world's population

questions.q: Four people are interviewed for a school magazine. Which one is a migrant in the sense used by the People of India project?
questions.a: The project's migrant is a person not living near the birthplace or with the original community, which fits the weaver who now lives and works in Surat, far from Odisha. The farmer still lives where he was born, the family moved only a street away in its own town, and the pilgrim goes back home after a week, so none of them is living away from the birthplace.
o: A weaver born in Odisha who now lives and works in Surat
A farmer who lives in the village where he was born
A family that moved one street away in its own town
A pilgrim who visits another State for a week, then returns

questions.q: (a) Using the chapter's figures, work out how many languages there are for each script, on average, in the People of India count. (b) What does your answer tell a classmate who assumes that every Indian language has a script of its own?
questions.a: (a) 325 languages / 25 scripts = 13 languages per script on average. (b) The assumption is wrong: there are far fewer scripts than languages, so on average many languages share one script.
s: Part (a): 325 / 25 = 13 languages per script
Part (b): scripts are far fewer than languages, so many languages share a script

questions.q:
Read the statements about the opening section of the chapter.
1. Vincent Smith, a British historian, wrote over a century ago that India offers unity in diversity.
2. The People of India project was carried out in the early 20th century.
3. The chapter says India's diversity is usually the first thing that strikes visitors.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are what the chapter says. Statement 2 is wrong: the Anthropological Survey of India conducted the project in the late 20th century.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A fact card in the school corridor reads: 'People of India project: surveyed 325 communities and counted 4,635 languages in 25 scripts.' What single correction makes the card match the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says the project surveyed 4,635 communities and counted 325 languages using 25 scripts, so the community and language figures have been swapped. Swapping the language and script figures on the card would give 25 languages and 4,635 scripts, which is also wrong; 18 is India's percentage of the world's population, not a count of scripts; and the 4,635 figure is a count of communities, not of States.
o: Swap the community and language figures
Swap the language and script figures with each other
Change the number of scripts from 25 to 18
Change 'communities' to 'States' in the first line

questions.q: India has over 1.4 billion people. Using the share of the world's population that the chapter gives for India, the world's population works out, to the nearest billion, to about ___ billion.
Kiran says, 'You only see India's diversity if you travel to another State.' Give two points from the chapter that show she is wrong.
questions.a: Any two: even within your own region you often meet people from other parts of India with different customs and traditions; the People of India project observed that many Indians may be called migrants, not living near their birthplace or with their original community; so people of different backgrounds already live side by side.
s: Point 1: within one's own region one meets people from other parts with different customs
Point 2: many Indians are migrants, living away from their birthplace or community

questions.q: Ayaan claims: 'The People of India project was a massive national survey, and its figures show that each of the communities it surveyed has a language of its own.' Test each part of his claim against the chapter's figures and give your verdict.
questions.a: No. The first part is right: the Anthropological Survey of India, a national organisation, carried out a massive survey of 4,635 communities across all States. The second part does not follow: the same survey counted only 325 languages, far fewer than 4,635 communities, so many communities must share a language and they cannot each have one of their own. Since the conclusion he draws is contradicted by the figures, the claim fails.
s: First part supported: a massive survey of 4,635 communities by a national organisation
Second part tested: 325 languages for 4,635 communities, so communities must share languages
Verdict: No, the conclusion is contradicted by the survey's own figures

questions.q: A debater argues: 'Unity in diversity is only a label that outsiders invented to make sense of a confusing country.' Her opponent wants a line from the chapter's opening pages that presents unity in diversity as something that has always belonged to India itself. Which line should he quote?
o: 'unity in diversity which has always been normal to [India]'
'How, in the face of such bewildering diversity, can a history of India be written?'
'it is usually the first thing that strikes visitors to our country'
'many Indians may be called migrants, in the sense of people not living near their birthplace'
questions.a: Sri Aurobindo's line, 'the principle of unity in diversity which has always been normal to [India]', presents it as India's own normal state. Vincent Smith's question is exactly an outsider puzzling over a 'bewildering' country, so it helps the debater rather than her opponent; the remark about visitors and the migrant finding are about diversity, not about where the idea of unity comes from.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter says that India's great diversity is not surprising.
Reason (R): The People of India project was conducted by the Anthropological Survey of India, a national organisation.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The chapter says diversity is not surprising because India has over 1.4 billion inhabitants, about 18 percent of the world's population. Who conducted the survey does not explain why diversity is to be expected.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
The register of Sunrise Apartments, Pune, lists its eight families. All members of each family were born in the same city.
F1 born Pune, home language Marathi (Devanagari script)
F2 born Pune, Marathi (Devanagari)
F3 born Patna, Hindi (Devanagari)
F4 born Kochi, Malayalam (Malayalam script)
F5 born Guwahati, Assamese (Assamese script)
F6 born Jaipur, Hindi (Devanagari)
F7 born Pune, Marathi (Devanagari)
F8 born Chennai, Tamil (Tamil script)
The society newsletter has one rule: no line may claim more than the evidence it quotes.
(a) How many families are migrants in the sense used by the People of India project?
(b) Which two home languages in the register share one script, and which finding of the People of India project does that repeat on a small scale?
(c) For the newsletter the secretary drafts Line X: 'Five of our eight families were born far from Pune, so most Indians today are migrants.' A resident offers Line Y: 'Five of our eight families were born far from Pune, a small example of what the People of India project observed across the country.' Which line should the newsletter print? Justify using (a) and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 5 families (F3, F4, F5, F6, F8), who live far from their birthplace. (b) Marathi and Hindi, both written in Devanagari; the project counted 325 languages but only 25 scripts, so languages share scripts. (c) Line Y. Line X is tempting because 5 of 8 is more than half, but eight families in one building cannot speak for the whole country, and the project itself, which surveyed 4,635 communities across all States, says only that many Indians may be called migrants, not most. Line Y uses the same count without claiming more than it shows, so it keeps the newsletter's rule.
s: Part (a): 5 migrant families
Part (b): Marathi and Hindi share Devanagari, as 325 languages share 25 scripts
Part (c): Line Y, since 8 families cannot stand for India and the project says 'many', not 'most'

questions.q: After Vincent Smith's question, the chapter asks, 'How shall we perceive and express this unity, or the Many in the One?' Which plan for the rest of the chapter matches how the chapter sets out to answer it?
questions.a: The chapter says, 'To answer this question, we will explore a few dimensions of Indian life', and then looks at food, clothing, festivals and literature for a common thread. It does not recount languages, does not choose one region as a standard, and does not stop at listing differences, which would show only diversity.
o: Look at food, dress, festivals and stories for a common thread
Count the 325 languages again, region by region, more carefully
Pick one region's customs and treat them as the standard for all
List every difference between regions and then stop there

questions.q: True or False? 'The chapter treats India's diversity as a problem that must be removed before India can be united.' Give the verdict and the reason from the chapter.
questions.a: False. The chapter says Indian culture celebrates diversity as an enrichment and never loses sight of the underlying unity which nourishes that diversity; its summary adds that diversity does not divide, it enriches.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: diversity is celebrated as an enrichment that does not divide, and unity nourishes it

questions.q: The chapter opens with a train journey through India. (a) List what the traveller notices changing along the way. (b) Which of these does the People of India project, as the chapter reports it, put numbers to? (c) What, then, does the journey show that the survey figures in the chapter do not?
questions.a: (a) Changing landscapes, different types of dresses and food, different languages (familiar and unfamiliar) and different scripts. (b) Languages and scripts: 325 languages using 25 scripts (the project also counted communities, 4,635 of them). (c) The changes in landscape, dress and food, which none of the chapter's figures measure, and the fact that diversity is something any visitor sees for himself, the first thing that strikes visitors.
s: Part (a): landscapes, dresses and food, languages and scripts
Part (b): languages and scripts are the ones the project counted
Part (c): landscape, dress and food are seen but not counted; diversity strikes any visitor

questions.q:
Match each line in Column A with the person in Column B who said or wrote it, as given in the chapter.
Column A: 1. 'I may never lose the bliss of the touch of the one in the play of the many.'  2. 'The Many in the One would place her on the sure foundation of her Swabhava and Swadharma.'  3. 'How, in the face of such bewildering diversity, can a history of India be written?'  4. 'There is hardly a place in the country which the epic heroes such as the Pandavas did not visit according to folklores.'
Column B: a. Vincent Smith  b. K.S. Singh  c. Rabindranath Tagore  d. Sri Aurobindo
questions.a: 1-c (Tagore's prayer), 2-d (Sri Aurobindo), 3-a (the British historian Vincent Smith), 4-b (the anthropologist K.S. Singh, who directed the People of India project).

questions.q: (a) Write the words in Tagore's opening line that name the one and the many. (b) Sri Aurobindo's phrase reverses Tagore's order of words. Explain how both lines still make the same point.
questions.a: (a) 'the touch of the one in the play of the many'. (b) Aurobindo writes 'the Many in the One'. Tagore begins with the one and Aurobindo with the many, but both say that a single underlying unity is present within all the variety, which is what the chapter calls unity in diversity.
s: Part (a): 'the one in the play of the many'
Part (b): reversed order, but both see one unity present inside the many

questions.q:
Sort the five statements below under three headings: (A) stated in the chapter, (B) a fair inference from the chapter, (C) goes beyond what the chapter says. Give a one-line reason for each.
1. The People of India project counted 325 languages.
2. Because the survey covered all States, its figures describe the whole country rather than a single region.
3. Most Indians today live in a different State from their parents.
4. India's diversity is usually the first thing that strikes visitors.
5. India has more languages than any other country in the world.
questions.a: 1 under (A): the chapter states it. 2 under (B): the chapter says the survey covered 4,635 communities across all States, so it follows that its figures are about the whole country, though the chapter does not put it in those words. 3 under (C): the chapter says only that many Indians may be called migrants; it gives no 'most', and says nothing about States or parents. 4 under (A): stated in the opening section. 5 under (C): the chapter gives India's own count of languages but compares it with no other country.
s: Statement 1 placed under stated, with reason
Statement 2 placed under inference: the survey covered all States
Statement 3 placed under goes beyond: 'many' is not 'most'
Statement 4 placed under stated
Statement 5 placed under goes beyond: no comparison with other countries

questions.q: In a project report Meghna writes: 'Vincent Smith believed a history of India could never be written because the country is too diverse.' Which point from the chapter shows that her summary is unfair to Smith?
questions.a: In the same quotation Smith answers his own question: 'The answer to the query is found in the fact that India offers unity in diversity.' The People of India project was directed by K.S. Singh, not Smith; Smith was a British historian, not an Indian one; and he wrote over a century ago, not in the late 20th century, so those options are not even true.
o: Smith answered his own question: unity in diversity
Smith directed the People of India project, which found unity
Smith was an Indian historian, so he had no difficulty at all
Smith wrote after the survey of 4,635 communities was finished

questions.q: The chapter calls India's diversity 'not surprising' and, a few lines later, says making sense of it is 'not so easy'. Give the reason the chapter offers for each of these two remarks.
questions.a: Not surprising: India has over 1.4 billion inhabitants, about 18 percent of the world's population. Not so easy: the diversity is so great (for instance 4,635 communities surveyed) that the historian Vincent Smith wondered how a history of such a 'bewildering' country could be written.
s: 'Not surprising': the population of over 1.4 billion, about 18 percent of the world
'Not so easy': the bewildering diversity that made Smith ask how its history could be written

questions.q: Write a three-line 'India in numbers' box for a school wall magazine. Each line must use a different figure from the chapter and say in a few words what that figure shows about India's diversity.
questions.a: For example: '1.4 billion people, about 18 percent of the world: diversity is not surprising in so large a population.' '4,635 communities surveyed across all States: India is made of thousands of distinct communities.' '325 languages in 25 scripts: languages far outnumber scripts, and both are many.' Any three correct figures, each with a correct meaning.
s: First correct figure with what it shows
Second, different figure with what it shows
Third, different figure with what it shows

questions.q:
Read this extract quoted in the chapter.
'How, in the face of such bewildering diversity, can a history of India be written? … The answer to the query is found in the fact that India offers unity in diversity.'
A debating team is using it to prepare a speech for the motion 'India's diversity is its strength'.
(a) Which word in the extract shows the writer found diversity hard to handle?
(b) One member wants to say: 'The writer was bewildered because he had read the People of India figure of 325 languages.' Using what the chapter says about the writer and about the project, show why this cannot be right.
(c) Another member wants to quote only the first sentence. Decide whether the team should quote the whole extract or only the first sentence, and justify your decision.
questions.a: (a) 'bewildering'. (b) The writer, the British historian Vincent Smith, wrote over a century ago, while the People of India project was carried out in the late 20th century, so its figure did not exist when he wrote. (c) Quote the whole extract. The first sentence alone only states the difficulty and would make diversity sound like an obstacle; the second sentence gives Smith's own answer, unity in diversity, which is exactly the chapter's view that diversity enriches rather than divides and so supports the motion.
s: Part (a): 'bewildering'
Part (b): Smith wrote over a century ago, the project came in the late 20th century
Part (c): whole extract, because the second sentence answers the difficulty with unity in diversity, which supports the motion

questions.q: 'The chapter does not stop at showing that India is diverse.' Justify this statement using the two opening quotations, Vincent Smith's question and the chapter's closing ideas.
questions.a: Tagore prays never to lose 'the touch of the one in the play of the many', and Sri Aurobindo speaks of 'the Many in the One', so from the first page the chapter looks for oneness inside variety. Smith asks how a history of so bewildering a country can be written and answers that India offers unity in diversity, which the chapter takes as its question to explore. It then studies a few dimensions of Indian life to find that unity. It closes by saying Indian culture celebrates diversity as an enrichment but never loses sight of the underlying unity that nourishes it, and that diversity does not divide but enriches. So diversity is the starting point, and unity is what the chapter sets out to show.
s: Tagore's line: the one in the play of the many
Aurobindo's line: the Many in the One
Smith's question and his answer, unity in diversity
The chapter explores dimensions of life to find the unity
Closing ideas: diversity as enrichment, nourished by an underlying unity

questions.q: Neha writes: 'Grains such as rice and wheat are common all over India, but the spices used are completely different from one region to the next.' Test both halves of her claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. The first half fits: the chapter says certain food grains, such as the cereals rice, barley and wheat, are common to almost every part of the country. The second half is wrong: the chapter says common spices such as turmeric, cumin, cardamom and ginger are used throughout the country.
s: Verdict: partly right
First half supported: staple grains common to almost every part of India
Second half corrected: turmeric, cumin, cardamom and ginger are used throughout the country

questions.q: A school canteen card lists three dishes: one made of rice, moong dal, turmeric and cumin; one of rice, chana dal and ginger; and one of wheat, moong dal, turmeric and ginger. Which idea from the chapter do the three dishes show together?
questions.a: The three dishes are different, yet they are made by combining the same few ingredients (rice, wheat, dals, turmeric, cumin, ginger): the same ingredients (unity) used in a number of combinations (diversity). The chapter says grains and spices are common across the country, that a dish's variety does not come from separate regional grain sets, and it never says spices make a grain a staple.
o: Shared ingredients combine into many dishes
Each region of India has its own separate set of grains
A grain becomes a staple grain when spices are added
Dishes are different because each uses a new spice

questions.q: True or False? 'According to the chapter, the things common to cooking across India are not limited to grains and spices.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. After naming staple grains and common spices, the chapter says we could continue the list with some common vegetables, common oils and so on.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the chapter says the list could continue with common vegetables and oils

questions.q:
A canteen in Bengaluru runs a 'Taste of India' week with one dish a day, each from a different region.
Monday: rice, moong dal, turmeric, cumin
Tuesday: wheat, chana dal, turmeric, ginger
Wednesday: ragi, cumin, ginger
Thursday: jowar, masoor dal, turmeric, cumin
Friday: barley, turmeric, ginger
The Social Science teacher will pin the week's poster beside the chapter as an example of both halves of 'unity in diversity'. The poster has room for one headline.
(a) On how many days is the dish built on a cereal, and on how many on a millet, by the chapter's headings?
(b) Which of the spices that the chapter says are used throughout the country does the week leave out?
(c) The canteen manager likes Headline X, 'One week, five regions, endless variety', because it sells the variety. The teacher suggests Headline Y, 'Five dishes, one shared store of grains and spices'. Which headline suits the teacher's purpose? Justify using (a) and (b).
questions.a: (a) Cereal on 3 days (rice, wheat, barley); millet on 2 days (ragi, jowar). (b) Cardamom. (c) Headline Y. Headline X is true and attractive, but it shows only the diversity. Headline Y shows both halves: five different dishes (diversity) built from the same staple grains, cereals and millets, and the same common spices (unity). One spice, cardamom, is missing this week, but every ingredient used comes from the shared list the chapter describes, so the store is still a shared one.
s: Part (a): cereal 3 days, millet 2 days
Part (b): cardamom
Part (c): Headline Y, because it shows shared ingredients as well as different dishes

questions.q:
Read the statements about food in the chapter.
1. The chapter gives maize, rice and wheat as its three examples of cereals.
2. Pearl millet, sorghum and finger millet are also known as bajra, jowar and ragi.
3. The chapter says turmeric, cumin, cardamom and ginger are used only in north India.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only statement 2 is correct. Statement 1 is wrong: the chapter's cereals are rice, barley and wheat (maize appears only as a label in a picture). Statement 3 is wrong: these spices are used throughout the country.
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A Class 6 chart sorts grains under the chapter's three headings: cereals, millets and pulses. Which row of the chart contains a mistake?
questions.a: Jowar (sorghum) is one of the chapter's millets, not a cereal; the chapter's cereals are rice, barley and wheat. The other rows match the chapter: bajra, ragi and jowar are millets, various dals and grams are pulses, and wheat, rice and barley are cereals.
o: Cereals: rice, barley, jowar
Millets: bajra, ragi, jowar
Pulses: various dals, grams
Cereals: wheat, rice and barley

questions.q: (a) A shop label reads 'Pearl millet (jowar)'. What is wrong with it, according to the chapter? (b) The shop wants a shelf of millets that matches the chapter. Which three labels should it carry, each with both names?
questions.a: (a) Pearl millet is bajra; jowar is sorghum, so the label pairs the wrong names. (b) Bajra (pearl millet), jowar (sorghum) and ragi (finger millet).
s: Part (a): pearl millet is bajra, jowar is sorghum
Part (b): bajra/pearl millet, jowar/sorghum, ragi/finger millet

questions.q: The chapter's figure, captioned 'A few examples of cereals and pulses from different regions of India', shows four separate heaps of rice labelled basmati, ponni, kollam and sona masuri. (a) What is the 'one' in these four heaps, and what is the 'many'? (b) The chapter's main food argument places the diversity in the dishes. How is the diversity in these four heaps different? (c) Does the figure support or weaken the claim that staple grains are common to almost every part of the country? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The one is a single cereal, rice; the many are its four varieties from different regions. (b) Here the diversity is inside one ingredient itself, a grain grown in regional varieties, not only in the way shared ingredients are combined into dishes. (c) It supports the claim: the same staple, rice, turns up in regions far apart, so the grain is common even where its variety differs.
s: Part (a): one cereal, rice; four regional varieties
Part (b): diversity within one ingredient, not only in combinations
Part (c): supports, the same staple is found in many regions

questions.q: A cook makes a mixed-flour roti from one of the cereals named in the text of the chapter and one of the millets named there. The number of different cereal-and-millet pairs she can choose from is ___.
A food magazine is checking four lines against the chapter before printing. Which line would the chapter NOT support?
questions.a: The chapter says the number of different dishes in India must be in the thousands, if not lakhs, so the regions do not all cook the same dishes. It does support the other three: common spices such as turmeric are used throughout, the list of common items could go on with vegetables and oils, and the grains are the basic food for most Indians.
o: Every region of India cooks the same dishes in the same way
Common spices such as turmeric are used throughout India
The list of common items could go on with vegetables and oils
Staple grains are the basic food of most people in India

questions.q:
A student filled in this table about food in the chapter. Check each row: say whether it is correct, and correct any row that is wrong.
Row 1. Cereals: rice, barley, wheat. What it shows: the basic food for most Indians.
Row 2. Millets: bajra = sorghum, jowar = pearl millet, ragi = finger millet.
Row 3. Pulses: various dals and grams. What it shows: eaten only in a few regions.
Row 4. Spices: turmeric, cumin, cardamom, ginger. What it shows: used throughout the country.
Row 5. Dishes: thousands, if not lakhs. What it shows: the unity of Indian food.
questions.a: Row 1 is correct: these cereals are staple grains, the basic food for most Indians. Row 2 is wrong: bajra is pearl millet and jowar is sorghum (ragi = finger millet is right). Row 3 is wrong: pulses are among the grains common to almost every part of the country. Row 4 is correct. Row 5 is wrong: the thousands of dishes show diversity; the unity lies in the shared ingredients.
s: Row 1 judged correct
Row 2 corrected: bajra is pearl millet, jowar is sorghum
Row 3 corrected: pulses are common to almost every part of India
Row 4 judged correct
Row 5 corrected: dishes show diversity, ingredients show unity

questions.q: (a) The chapter names four spices used throughout India. If a cook uses exactly two of them in a dish, how many different pairs of spices can she choose? (b) What does your answer suggest about the chapter's phrase 'an endless variety of dishes'?
questions.a: (a) Turmeric, cumin, cardamom and ginger give 6 pairs (4 x 3 / 2 = 6). (b) Even four common spices give six different pairs; combined with the staple grains, vegetables and oils, a small common set of ingredients can be combined in so many ways that the dishes become almost endless.
s: Part (a): 6 pairs from the four named spices
Part (b): a few common ingredients give very many combinations, hence endless variety

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Turmeric is on the chapter's list of things used throughout India, but it is not on its list of staple grains.
Reason (R): The chapter's staple grains are cereals, millets and pulses, the basic food for most Indians, while turmeric is one of its common spices.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The chapter names cereals, millets and pulses as staple grains, the basic food for most Indians, and names turmeric among the common spices used throughout the country; turmeric is left off the staple-grain list because it is a spice, not a grain.

questions.q: A student writes in her notebook: 'Rice, wheat and dals are eaten in every single part of India.' Which word in the chapter's account of food shows that she has gone further than the book?
o: almost, as in 'almost every part'
basic, as in 'the basic food' of Indians
endless, as in 'an endless variety of dishes'
throughout, as in 'used throughout the country'
questions.a: The chapter says certain food grains are common to 'almost every part of the country', not to every single part, so 'almost' is the word she has dropped. 'Basic' describes what staple grains are, 'endless' describes the dishes, and 'throughout' is said of the common spices, so none of them limits her claim about grains.

questions.q: A quiz-master's rough working reads: '3 + 3 + 4 = 10, against thousands, if not lakhs.' Write a question about the chapter's food section that this working answers, say what the 3, the 3 and the 4 stand for, and explain what the comparison shows.
questions.a: For example: 'How many cereals, millets and spices does the chapter name, and how does that compare with the number of dishes in India?' The 3 are the cereals rice, barley and wheat; the next 3 the millets bajra, jowar and ragi; the 4 the spices turmeric, cumin, cardamom and ginger (the pulses are given only as 'various dals and grams'). About ten named ingredients against dishes in their thousands, if not lakhs, shows a short shared list (unity) giving rise to a huge number of dishes (diversity).
s: A suitable question about named ingredients and the number of dishes
3 cereals, 3 millets and 4 spices identified
Comparison: a short shared list against thousands of dishes, unity and diversity

questions.q: (a) In the chapter's food section the unity lies in shared ingredients. What plays the same part in its section on the sari? (b) What in the sari section plays the part of the 'thousands, if not lakhs' of dishes?
questions.a: (a) The sari itself: one plain, unstitched length of cloth worn in most parts of India, whatever the material. (b) Its hundreds of varieties: different fabrics (cotton, silk, synthetic), methods of weaving and designing, endless colours, and the many ways of draping it.
s: Part (a): the single unstitched sari worn in most of India
Part (b): its many fabrics, weaves, designs, colours and drapes

questions.q:
A grain stall at a fair in Hyderabad has these prices per kg: rice Rs 60, wheat Rs 40, barley Rs 70, bajra Rs 50, jowar Rs 55, ragi Rs 65, moong dal Rs 120, chana dal Rs 90. A family from Tamil Nadu bought exactly 1 kg of one cereal, 1 kg of one millet and 1 kg of one dal, and paid Rs 205 in all.
(a) Which three items on the list are millets?
(b) Work backwards to find exactly which three items the family bought.
(c) Under which name does the chapter also know the millet they bought?
(d) The stall-keeper told them, 'These are grains of the north; you won't use them at home.' Judge his remark using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Bajra, jowar and ragi. (b) Rice (60) + jowar (55) + chana dal (90) = Rs 205; no other cereal-millet-dal choice adds up to 205. (c) Sorghum. (d) He is wrong: the chapter says these staple grains (cereals, millets and pulses) are common to almost every part of the country, so they are used in Tamil Nadu as much as in the north.
s: Part (a): bajra, jowar and ragi
Part (b): rice, jowar and chana dal, 60 + 55 + 90 = 205
Part (c): sorghum
Part (d): wrong, staple grains are common to almost every part of India

questions.q: Ananya says ragi cannot be a staple grain because it is a millet, not a cereal. Which point from the chapter corrects her?
o: Cereals, millets and pulses all count as staple grains
Ragi is really a cereal, so it is a staple grain after all
Only grains cooked with common spices are staple grains
Ragi is a pulse, so it belongs with chana and moong dal
questions.a: The chapter lists cereals (rice, barley, wheat), millets (bajra, jowar, ragi) and pulses (dals and grams) and says all these are called staple grains because they are the basic food for most Indians, so a millet is a staple grain too. Ragi is finger millet, neither a cereal nor a pulse, and the chapter never ties the word 'staple' to spices.

questions.q: A traveller eats a different dish in every State she visits. Give two reasons from the chapter why she is still, in one sense, eating 'the same' food everywhere.
questions.a: The staple grains (cereals such as rice, barley and wheat, millets such as bajra, jowar and ragi, and dals and grams) are common to almost every part of the country; and common spices such as turmeric, cumin, cardamom and ginger are used throughout India.
s: Staple grains common to almost every part of India
Common spices used throughout the country

questions.q: A school exhibition captioned 'Cereals and pulses of India' shows exactly these nine labelled heaps: basmati rice, ponni rice, wheat, jowar, ragi, chana dal, moong dal, masoor dal and arhar dal. (a) Sort the heaps under the chapter's three headings for staple grains and give the count for each heading. (b) Which heaps does the caption leave out, judged by the chapter's headings? (c) Which grain named in the text of the chapter is missing from the cereals on show, and which from the millets?
questions.a: (a) Cereals 3 (basmati rice, ponni rice, wheat); millets 2 (jowar, ragi); pulses 4 (chana, moong, masoor and arhar dal). (b) Jowar and ragi: they are millets, neither cereals nor pulses, so 'Cereals and pulses' does not cover them. (c) Barley is the missing cereal; bajra (pearl millet) is the missing millet.
s: Part (a): cereals 3, millets 2, pulses 4
Part (b): jowar and ragi, the millets
Part (c): barley and bajra

questions.q: 'Indian food is a good example of the Many in the One.' Justify this statement from the chapter, and explain why the huge number of dishes in India does not weaken the argument.
questions.a: The One: certain food grains are common to almost every part of the country, cereals (rice, barley, wheat), millets (bajra, jowar, ragi) and pulses (dals and grams), the staple grains that are the basic food for most Indians. Common spices such as turmeric, cumin, cardamom and ginger are used throughout, and the list could go on with vegetables and oils. The Many: these same ingredients are combined in a number of ways into dishes that run into thousands, if not lakhs. The large number of dishes does not weaken the argument; it is the 'many' half of it, because all those dishes come from the same shared ingredients.
s: Staple grains common to almost every part of India
Common spices used throughout, list could go on
Same ingredients combined in many ways
Dishes run into thousands, if not lakhs: the many
The number of dishes is the diversity half, so it supports the argument

questions.q:
Read the statements about the sari in the chapter.
1. Some sari designs are part of the cloth, while others are printed after the cloth is woven.
2. The chapter names Paithani and Patan Patola among famous silk saris and says there are many more kinds of cotton saris.
3. In past centuries, travellers to India marvelled at the sari's simplicity and economy.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: All three statements are correct: each is what the chapter says about the sari's designs, its famous silk types and cotton varieties, and what travellers admired.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q:
A school museum corner in Patna has room for only one exhibit under the label 'The sari's long history'.
Exhibit P: a photograph of the stone relief from Vaishali showing a woman in a sari.
Exhibit Q: a printed copy of an old traveller's account, from a past century, praising the sari's simplicity, its economy and the many ways it is worn.
(a) To roughly what period does the chapter date Exhibit P, and what does the relief show?
(b) A second panel is called 'One dress, many ways'. Which exhibit belongs there, and which part of its content fits that title?
(c) A visitor argues that Exhibit Q should go under 'The sari's long history', because a written account is easier to read than a carving. Decide which exhibit belongs under that label, and justify using (a) and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) A few centuries BCE; a woman wearing a sari, carved in stone. (b) Exhibit Q: its praise of the many ways the sari is worn. (c) Exhibit P. The written account is easier to read and it does come from the past, but the chapter itself offers the Vaishali relief as its evidence that 'the sari has a long history', reaching back a few centuries BCE. The travellers are placed only in 'past centuries', and what they recorded, the sari's simplicity, economy and diverse drapes, is what the second panel is about.
s: Part (a): a few centuries BCE, a woman in a sari carved in stone
Part (b): Exhibit Q, the many ways of wearing it
Part (c): Exhibit P, the chapter's own evidence of a long history, reaching back a few centuries BCE

questions.q: A museum guide points at the stone relief from Vaishali and says, 'This proves that Indian cloth was sold in Europe.' Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter uses the Vaishali relief, which goes back a few centuries BCE, as evidence of the sari's long history; its evidence for textiles reaching Europe is chintz in the 17th century. The relief is not from the 17th century, it is not described as a Banarasi silk sari or as a sale, and the chapter never says saris were first worn only in Bihar.
o: It shows the sari's long history; chintz shows the trade
It is from the 17th century, when chintz was sent to Europe
It shows a Banarasi silk sari being sold to a European buyer
It shows that the sari was first worn only in today's Bihar

questions.q: True or False? 'A sari counts as one and the same dress only if it is draped in the same way everywhere.' Give the verdict and the reason or correction from the chapter.
questions.a: False. The chapter says there are many ways of wearing the sari, varying from region to region and community to community, and new ways of draping it are still being invented, but in the end it is a single dress, the sari.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: many drapes, still being invented, yet a single dress

questions.q: A weaver explains to visitors why there are hundreds of varieties of sari. Which reason she gives would the chapter NOT support?
questions.a: The chapter calls the sari an unstitched piece of cloth, so its variety cannot come from stitching. It does name the other three: different fabrics (cotton, silk, synthetic), designs woven into the cloth or printed after weaving, and endless colours from many kinds of pigments.
o: It is stitched in a different pattern in each region
It is made in cotton, in silk and in synthetic fabric
Its designs are woven into it or printed after weaving
Its colours come from many different kinds of pigments

questions.q: Arjun claims: 'Indian printed cotton was so much in demand in 17th-century Europe that two European countries decided to stop it from being imported.' Test his claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: Yes, the claim is supported. The chapter says a printed Indian cotton called chintz became so popular in 17th-century Europe that the sale of some European dresses dropped sharply. To protect their own products, England and France decided to ban the import of chintz from India. So the demand was real and the two countries did act to stop the imports.
s: Chintz was so popular in 17th-century Europe that European dress sales dropped
England and France decided to ban its import to protect their own products
Verdict: Yes, the claim is supported

questions.q: Two cotton saris have the same colour, the same flower pattern and the same drape. The only difference: on one, the flowers were made on the loom as part of the cloth; on the other, they were added after the cloth was woven. By the chapter's account of how saris are designed, the second sari's flowers are ___.
questions.a: printed

questions.q: (a) The chapter says the Vaishali relief goes back 'a few centuries BCE'. Suppose a museum label dates it to 300 BCE. How many years before 2026 is that? (Remember there is no year zero.) (b) What does the relief tell us about the sari?
questions.a: (a) 300 + 2026 - 1 = 2,325 years. (b) The sari has a long history: a woman wearing one was carved in stone more than two thousand years ago.
s: Part (b): the sari has been worn for over two thousand years, a long history

questions.q: A pen-friend from France writes to you: 'People in my country never cared for Indian cloth. And your sari is just one plain garment, made and worn the same way everywhere.' Write a reply that corrects him on five points, using the chapter.
questions.a: A reply making five correct points, for example: (1) For a very long time India produced the finest cotton in the world and its textiles reached Europe. (2) A printed cotton called chintz became so popular in 17th-century Europe that the sale of some European dresses dropped sharply. (3) France and England even decided to ban chintz to protect their own products, which shows how much it was wanted. (4) The sari is one dress, but it is made of cotton, silk (Banarasi, Kanjivaram, Paithani, Patan Patola, Muga, Mysore) or synthetic fabric, by different methods of weaving and designing, in endless colours. (5) It is draped in many ways that vary by region and community, and new drapes are still being invented.
s: India's fine cotton textiles reached Europe
Chintz so popular that European dress sales dropped
France and England banned chintz to protect their own products
The sari's many fabrics, weaves, designs and colours
The sari's many drapes, still being invented

questions.q: At a fashion show in Mumbai, a designer drapes a sari in a style no one has seen before. How would the chapter describe what she is wearing?
questions.a: The chapter says there are many ways of wearing the sari, that new ways of draping it are still being invented, and that in the end it is a single dress, the sari. A sari is not defined by one fixed drape, travellers praised the many ways it is worn, and a new drape needs no new fabric.
o: Still one dress, the sari, in a newly invented drape
A new dress, since a sari is fixed by one way of draping
Not a sari, since travellers praised only the old drapes
A synthetic sari, since a new drape needs a new fabric

questions.q: (a) Name the two ways the chapter says designs get onto a sari. (b) Explain how these, together with colour, give one dress hundreds of varieties.
questions.a: (a) Some designs are part of the cloth, made while weaving; others are printed after the cloth is woven. (b) Each design method can be combined with endless colours from many kinds of pigments, and with different fabrics and weaving methods, so the single dress comes in hundreds of varieties.
s: Part (a): designs woven in, or printed after weaving
Part (b): combined with endless colours and fabrics, hundreds of varieties result

questions.q:
Assertion (A): England and France banned the import of chintz from India because it had become unpopular in Europe.
Reason (R): Chintz became so popular in 17th-century Europe that the sale of some European dresses dropped sharply.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. Chintz was banned because it was so popular: to protect their own products, England and France decided to ban its import.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: The chapter calls the sari 'a single dress' and also says it comes in 'hundreds of varieties'. Interpret how both can be true, using three points from the chapter.
questions.a: It is one dress because it is the same plain, unstitched length of cloth worn in most parts of India, and however it is draped, in the end it is a single dress. It comes in hundreds of varieties because it is made of different fabrics (cotton, silk such as Banarasi or Kanjivaram, and synthetic), by different methods of weaving and designing, and in endless colours. So the form is shared (unity) and the making and wearing vary (diversity).
s: One dress: the same unstitched length of cloth worn in most of India
Varieties from fabrics, weaving and designing methods, and colours
Draping differs yet it stays one dress: unity in diversity

questions.q: A cloth merchant in 17th-century Europe complains in a letter that his dresses are selling far less than before. Which development described in the chapter best explains his complaint?
questions.a: Chintz, a printed Indian cotton, became so popular in 17th-century Europe that the sale of some European dresses dropped sharply. The ban by England and France came later and was meant to protect European products, so it would help him rather than cause his loss; the chapter says Indian textiles reached as far as Europe; and chintz was cotton, not silk.
o: Chintz grew so popular that European dresses sold less
England and France banned the import of chintz from India
Indian textiles were sent only as far as Southeast Asia
Indian silk saris replaced the dresses sold in his shop

questions.q: A classmate says: 'India has six kinds of sari: Banarasi, Kanjivaram, Paithani, Patan Patola, Muga and Mysore.' (a) Give two things the chapter says that show she has undercounted. (b) Which fabric do all six of her names belong to, and which two fabrics does her list leave out?
questions.a: (a) Any two: the six are only some of the famous types of silk saris; there are many more kinds of cotton saris; altogether the sari comes in hundreds of varieties. (b) Silk; her list leaves out cotton and synthetic saris.
s: Part (a): famous silk types only, many more cotton kinds, hundreds of varieties (any two)
Part (b): silk; cotton and synthetic left out

questions.q:
Read this imaginary traveller's diary, written for this question.
Line 1: 'The women here wear one long piece of cloth, with no stitching at all.'
Line 2: 'It needs no tailor, so even a poor family can afford it.'
Line 3: 'In the river town it was draped one way; two days' ride west, quite another.'
Line 4: 'I conclude that each region drapes the cloth in its own way, so a woman's drape tells you exactly which region she comes from.'
(a) The chapter says travellers marvelled at the sari's simplicity, economy and diverse ways of wearing it. Which of these three does Line 2 show?
(b) Line 3 records one source of the sari's variety. Name two other sources of variety the chapter gives that the traveller, watching only how it was draped, did not record.
(c) Judge the traveller's conclusion in Line 4 using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Economy. (b) Any two: different fabrics (cotton, silk, synthetic); different methods of weaving and designing (designs woven in or printed after weaving); endless colours from many kinds of pigments. (c) Partly right. The chapter agrees that ways of wearing the sari vary from one region to another. But it says they also vary from one community to another, and that new ways of draping are still being invented, so a drape cannot tell you exactly which region a woman comes from. And whatever the drape, it remains a single dress, the sari.
s: Part (a): economy
Part (b): two of fabrics, weaving and designing methods, colours
Part (c): partly right, drapes vary by region but also by community and new drapes appear, so not exact

questions.q:
Match each idea about Indian textiles in Column A with the evidence the chapter gives for it in Column B.
Column A: 1. The sari has a long history  2. Indian textiles reached Europe  3. The sari's variety comes partly from how it is made  4. The sari is put to uses beyond a dress
Column B: a. Pictures from south India of women using the sari in creative ways  b. A stone relief from Vaishali, a few centuries BCE  c. England and France banning chintz in the 17th century  d. Designs woven into the cloth or printed after weaving
questions.a: 1-b (the Vaishali relief), 2-c (chintz was popular enough in Europe to be banned), 3-d (methods of weaving and designing), 4-a (the pictures of creative uses).

questions.q: The chapter says every region and community in India has developed its own styles of clothing, yet it also speaks of a 'commonality'. Explain both halves using the sari.
questions.a: Diversity: clothing styles differ by region and community, and even the sari is woven, designed, coloured and draped differently. Commonality: the sari itself, a plain unstitched length of cloth, is worn in most parts of India irrespective of the material used.
s: Diversity: own styles, and many sari weaves, designs, colours and drapes
Commonality: the same unstitched sari worn in most parts of India, whatever the material

questions.q: Three sisters attend a wedding: one in a Kanjivaram silk sari, one in a plain cotton sari and one in a synthetic sari. Which point does the chapter make with examples like this?
questions.a: The chapter says we notice a commonality in some traditional Indian dresses irrespective of the material used, and gives the sari, made mostly of cotton or silk and nowadays synthetic fabric too. It does not say only silk saris count, it treats synthetic as a newer fabric, and three fabrics of one sari show a shared dress, not three different dresses.
o: One common dress, whatever the material
Only a silk sari counts as a traditional dress
Synthetic saris are the oldest kind of sari
Each fabric makes the sari a different dress

questions.q: Three saris are laid out in class: (i) a red Kanjivaram silk sari; (ii) a red cotton sari with the same woven pattern; (iii) the sari from (i), now draped in a different regional style. Using the chapter, say what makes (i) and (ii) different varieties, what makes (i) and (iii) look different, and why all three are still one dress.
questions.a: (i) and (ii) differ in fabric: the chapter says saris are made from different fabrics, mostly cotton or silk. (i) and (iii) are the very same cloth and differ only in the way of wearing it; the chapter says ways of wearing the sari vary from one region to another and from one community to another. All three are the same plain, unstitched length of cloth, and however it is made or draped, in the end it is a single dress, the sari.
s: (i) and (ii): different fabric, silk and cotton
(i) and (iii): same cloth, a different regional drape
All three: one unstitched length of cloth, a single dress

questions.q: (a) Why would a 17th-century English cloth-maker have welcomed the ban on chintz from India? (b) What does the very need for such a ban show about Indian cotton at that time, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) Chintz had become so popular in Europe that the sale of some European dresses dropped sharply; England and France banned its import to protect their own products, so the ban protected his trade. (b) Indian cotton was so fine and so much wanted that it threatened Europe's own cloth trade; the chapter says that for a very long time India produced the finest cotton in the world.
s: Part (a): chintz had cut European dress sales, the ban protected their own products
Part (b): Indian cotton was the finest and in such demand that it threatened European cloth

questions.q:
A student made this flow chart of the chintz story:
Box 1: For a very long time India produced the finest cotton in the world.
Box 2: A printed cotton called chintz was exported as far as Europe.
Box 3: Chintz became very popular in 17th-century Europe.
Box 4: As a result, the sale of some European dresses rose sharply.
Box 5: England and France banned chintz to help Indian weavers.
(a) Find the two boxes that do not match the chapter and correct each. (b) What does the corrected chain show about India's textiles at the time?
questions.a: (a) Box 4 is wrong: the sale of some European dresses dropped sharply, it did not rise. Box 5 is wrong: England and France banned chintz to protect their own products, not to help Indian weavers. Boxes 1, 2 and 3 are correct. (b) Indian cotton textiles were so fine and so much in demand that they hurt European cloth sales and made two countries ban them.
s: Box 4 identified as wrong
Box 4 corrected: European dress sales dropped sharply
Box 5 identified as wrong
Box 5 corrected: banned to protect their own products
Part (b): Indian textiles were fine and in such demand they threatened European trade

questions.q: A school calendar marks four harvest celebrations of its students' families. Which one could NOT belong to the group of festivals the chapter describes with Makara Sankranti?
questions.a: The chapter says Makara Sankranti marks the beginning of the harvest season on or around January 14, and its map shows names of similar festivals about the same date. A festival in mid-October is far from that date; January 13, 14 and 15 are all 'around January 14'.
o: A harvest feast held on 15 October
A harvest festival held on 13 January
A harvest festival held on 14 January
A harvest festival held on 15 January

questions.q: Sana claims: 'The chapter describes only one festival in detail, so India must have rather few festivals, and most of them are Makara Sankranti under different names.' Test her claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: No. The chapter says there is an immense variety of festivals in India. It says only a few common ones are celebrated across India almost at the same time under different names, and it takes Makara Sankranti as 'just one example' of these. Describing one example in detail does not mean there are few festivals; it is a way of showing the pattern clearly.
s: The chapter: an immense variety of festivals in India
Makara Sankranti is just one example of a few common festivals with different names
Verdict: No, one detailed example does not mean few festivals

questions.q: Makara Sankranti is one occasion known by different names in different places. Which pair from elsewhere in the chapter is likewise one thing with two names, rather than two different things?
o: Bajra and pearl millet
Banarasi and Kanjivaram saris
Rice and wheat, both cereals
The Ramayana and the Mahabharata
questions.a: Bajra is the chapter's other name for pearl millet: one grain, two names, just as similar mid-January festivals carry different names. Banarasi and Kanjivaram are two different types of silk sari, rice and wheat are two different cereals, and the two epics are two different stories.

questions.q:
A school in Bhopal is planning a mid-January assembly. Class 7B lists what each student's family calls its festival at that time: Pongal 3 students, Uttarayan 2, Maghi/Lohri 4, Magh Bihu 1, Khichdi Parv 2, Makar Sankranti 5. The principal wants the banner to make the same point that the chapter makes with this festival.
(a) How many of the 17 students' families celebrate a festival whose name appears on the chapter's map, and what does the chapter say the festival marks?
(b) Raghav says Khichdi Parv cannot belong with the others because its name has nothing in common with 'Sankranti'. Answer him using the chapter.
(c) The banner can carry one title: Title X, 'Makar Sankranti Day', the name used most in the class, or Title Y, 'One harvest festival, many names'. Which title meets the principal's aim? Justify using the class figures.
questions.a: (a) All 17: Pongal, Uttarayan, Maghi/Lohri, Magh Bihu, Khichdi Parv and Makar Sankranti are all names on the map. The festival marks the beginning of the harvest season in many parts of India. (b) The chapter's map shows Khichdi Parv among the different names of similar festivals held across India about the same date; a different name is exactly the diversity the chapter describes, not a sign of a different occasion. (c) Title Y. Title X uses the single most common name, but only 5 of the 17 students know the festival by it, so 12 would not see their own name. The chapter's point is that a few common festivals are celebrated across India at almost the same time under different names, and Title Y says exactly that.
s: Part (a): all 17; the beginning of the harvest season
Part (b): Khichdi Parv is on the map; different names are the diversity
Part (c): Title Y, since only 5 of 17 use Title X's name and the chapter's point is one festival under many names

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Pongal and Uttarayan both appear on the chapter's map of similar festivals.
Reason (R): Both are celebrated in October-November, when many major festivals take place in India.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. The map shows names of festivals similar to Makara Sankranti, held about the same date, on or around January 14, not in October-November.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A student writes that Makara Sankranti and the similar festivals on the chapter's map fall in mid-January because that is when seeds are sown in many parts of India. Which correction matches the chapter?
o: It marks the beginning of the harvest season
It marks the end of the harvest season instead
It marks the sowing of seeds in every part of India
It marks the start of the October-November festivals
questions.a: The chapter says Makara Sankranti marks the beginning of the harvest season in many parts of India on or around January 14, so it is about gathering crops, not sowing them. It does not speak of the end of the harvest, never says 'every part', and the October-November festivals are a separate group mentioned only in an activity.

questions.q: A school in Delhi has students from many States. Write a three- or four-line invitation to a mid-January 'Harvest Festival of India' event that uses at least three names from the chapter's map and states correctly what the festival marks and when.
questions.a: Any invitation that correctly uses three or more map names and the chapter's facts, for example: 'Join us on 14 January to celebrate Makara Sankranti, Pongal, Uttarayan, Magh Bihu and Maghi/Lohri together! In many parts of India, this day marks the beginning of the harvest season. Different names, one celebration.'
s: Uses at least three names shown on the chapter's map
States that it marks the beginning of the harvest season
Gives the date as on or around January 14

questions.q: Pongal, Uttarayan and Magh Bihu fall at about the same time of year and mark the same occasion; according to the chapter, what differs among them is their ___.
questions.a: names

questions.q:
Complete this table from the chapter. For each row write what stays the same (unity) and what varies (diversity). Then write one sentence on what all four rows have in common.
Row 1: Food
Row 2: The sari
Row 3: Makara Sankranti
Row 4: The Panchatantra
questions.a: Food: the same staple grains and spices / the thousands of dishes made from them. Sari: one unstitched length of cloth, one dress / fabrics, weaves, designs, colours and drapes. Makara Sankranti: the same occasion, the beginning of the harvest season, on or around January 14 / many regional names such as Pongal, Uttarayan, Magh Bihu. Panchatantra: one collection of animal stories / about 200 adaptations in more than 50 languages. Common to all: one shared thing takes many forms, which is the 'Many in the One'.
s: Food row: same grains and spices, many dishes
Sari row: one dress, many fabrics, designs and drapes
Makara Sankranti row: same occasion and date, many names
Panchatantra row: one collection, many adaptations
Common sentence: one shared thing in many forms

questions.q: Makara Sankranti is one occasion known by many regional names. Which other example from the chapter follows the same pattern of one shared thing appearing in many regional forms?
questions.a: The sari is one dress worn in many regional and community drapes, the same 'one in many forms' pattern. The chintz ban, the count of 25 scripts and the date of the Vaishali relief are facts from the chapter, but none of them is one thing taking many regional forms.
o: The sari, one dress worn in many regional drapes
The chintz ban by England and France in Europe
The 25 scripts counted by the People of India project
The date of the Vaishali relief, a few centuries BCE

questions.q:
An imaginary newspaper report, written for this question, begins: 'On this cold winter morning, as farmers in many parts of the country begin their harvest, families from west to east celebrate one festival under many names.' The date has been torn off. For space, the editor must cut one of the two sentences in the next paragraph:
S1: 'Across India the festival goes by many names, yet it is one celebration.'
S2: 'The festival marks the beginning of the harvest season.'
(a) Work backwards: around which date was the report written?
(b) Give two names, other than Makara Sankranti, that the reporter could print, taken from the chapter's map.
(c) The editor's rule is to keep the sentence that shows the chapter's idea of unity in diversity. Which sentence should he keep? Justify.
questions.a: (a) On or around January 14: a winter festival at the beginning of the harvest season, under many names, is the chapter's Makara Sankranti. (b) Any two of Pongal, Makara Sankramana, Makara Vilakku, Makar Sankraat, Khichdi Parv, Uttarayan, Maghi/Lohri, Shishur Saenkraat, Magh Bihu, Pedda Panduga, Poush Songkranti. (c) S1. Both sentences are true to the chapter, but S2 gives only the shared occasion, which the opening line already reports. S1 carries both halves: many names (diversity) and one celebration (unity), which is the chapter's reason for choosing this festival.
s: Part (a): on or around January 14
Part (b): two correct names from the map
Part (c): S1, it shows both many names and one celebration; S2 only repeats the occasion

questions.q:
Read the statements about festivals in the chapter.
1. The chapter's map shows the names of festivals that fall in October-November.
2. The chapter says a few common festivals are celebrated across India almost at the same time, though under different names.
3. Uttarayan and Magh Bihu are among the names shown on the chapter's map.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is wrong: the map shows names of similar festivals about the same date as Makara Sankranti, on or around January 14. October-November festivals are only mentioned in an activity.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 only

questions.q: A student writes: 'Makara Sankranti marks the beginning of the harvest season in every part of India.' One word makes the sentence go beyond the chapter. Which change fixes it?
questions.a: The chapter says Makara Sankranti marks the beginning of the harvest season in many parts of India, so 'every' must become 'many'. It does mark the beginning of the harvest season, so 'harvest' and 'beginning' are right, and the chapter's map shows names across India, not only in the south.
o: Change 'every' to 'many'
Change 'harvest' to 'sowing'
Change 'beginning' to 'end'
Change 'India' to 'south India'

questions.q: K.S. Singh observed that, according to folklore, there is hardly a place in the country the epic heroes did not visit; the chapter's festival map shows names spread across the country. Interpret (i) what is shared across India in each case, (ii) how the diversity shows in each, and (iii) which of the two the chapter ties to a particular time of year.
questions.a: (i) Epics: the same heroes and stories; festival: the same occasion, the beginning of the harvest season. (ii) Epics: countless folk and tribal versions and local legends of the heroes visiting a community's own region; festival: many different regional names. (iii) The festival, celebrated on or around January 14.
s: (i) same heroes and stories; same harvest occasion
(ii) many folk versions and local legends; many regional names
(iii) the festival, on or around January 14

questions.q: 'The chapter's short section on festivals is a small copy of the argument of the whole chapter.' Justify this statement, setting what the festival section says beside the chapter's closing ideas.
questions.a: The whole chapter says diversity is easy to perceive, that there is also an underlying unity, and that diversity does not divide but enriches. The festival section follows the same steps. It opens with diversity: an immense variety of festivals in India. It then finds the unity: a few common festivals are celebrated across India almost at the same time. It gives one example, Makara Sankranti, marking the beginning of the harvest season in many parts of India on or around January 14. It shows the diversity inside that unity: the map gives many names, such as Pongal, Uttarayan, Magh Bihu and Pedda Panduga. So, like the chapter, it moves from visible diversity to the unity beneath it, and the many names enrich the one occasion rather than dividing it.
s: Chapter's closing ideas: diversity easy to see, an underlying unity, diversity enriches
Festival section opens with an immense variety of festivals
Unity: a few common festivals at almost the same time, Makara Sankranti as the example
Diversity inside the unity: many regional names on the map
Judgement: same movement from visible diversity to underlying unity

questions.q: True or False? 'The chapter suggests that Makara Sankranti is not the only festival celebrated across India at about the same time under different names.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says a few common festivals are celebrated across India almost at the same time, though they have different names, and then says it will take 'just one example', Makara Sankranti.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: 'a few common ones', of which Makara Sankranti is just one example

questions.q: (a) For Makara Sankranti and for the Panchatantra, say what the chapter treats as the 'one' in each. (b) Using (a), explain one way in which the 'many' arises differently in the two cases.
questions.a: (a) Makara Sankranti: one occasion, the beginning of the harvest season on or around January 14. Panchatantra: one original Sanskrit collection of animal stories. (b) The festival's 'many' are different regional names for similar festivals held at about the same time; the Panchatantra's 'many' are about 200 adaptations in more than 50 languages, made over centuries and carried beyond India, inspiring new collections on the way.
s: Part (a): one harvest occasion; one Sanskrit collection
Part (b): many names at one time, against many adaptations spread over centuries and languages

questions.q: Differentiate how the chapter finds unity in Indian food and in Makara Sankranti, and say what plays the part of diversity in each.
questions.a: Food: the unity is the shared ingredients, staple grains and common spices used across the country; the diversity is the thousands of dishes made from them. Makara Sankranti: the unity is the same occasion, the beginning of the harvest season, on about the same date, around January 14; the diversity is the many regional names it goes by.
s: Food: shared ingredients as unity, many dishes as diversity
Festival: same occasion and date as unity, many names as diversity

questions.q: (a) Vincent Smith wrote of India's 'bewildering diversity'. Why might the chapter's festival map, at first glance, seem to bear out his word? (b) What does a closer look at the map show that matches his own answer to his question?
questions.a: (a) The map shows more than ten different names spread across the country, which at first look like many unrelated festivals. (b) The names belong to similar festivals held about the same date, around January 14, marking the same occasion: unity in diversity, which is the answer Smith himself gave.
s: Part (a): many different names across India look like many unrelated festivals
Part (b): similar festivals on about the same date, unity in diversity, Smith's answer

questions.q: (a) Using a finding of the People of India project, explain why a family that celebrates Magh Bihu might be living among neighbours who celebrate Pongal. (b) What might the family discover about the two festivals, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) The project observed that many Indians may be called migrants, people not living near their birthplace or with their original community, so families from different regions often live side by side. (b) That the two are similar festivals held about the same date, around January 14, under different names: unity in diversity.
s: Part (a): many Indians are migrants living away from their birthplace or community
Part (b): similar festivals about the same date with different names

questions.q: (a) The chapter calls Indian literatures 'extremely diverse'. Name the two kinds of difference among them that it mentions by name. (b) Using the Panchatantra, explain what these literatures still share despite those differences.
questions.a: (a) Differences in language and in technique. (b) Important themes and concerns: the same animal stories, teaching the same important life skills, have been adapted in almost every Indian language, so literatures that differ in language and telling still share them.
s: Part (a): language and technique
Part (b): shared themes, the same stories and lessons across almost every Indian language

questions.q: True or False? 'A reader in Europe today could be enjoying stories whose roots lie in a collection first composed in India more than 2,000 years ago.' Give the verdict and the reason from the chapter.
questions.a: True. The original Sanskrit text of the Panchatantra is at least 2,200 years old, and its stories travelled all the way to Europe, inspiring new collections of stories on the way.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the Sanskrit original is at least 2,200 years old and its stories reached Europe

questions.q: A librarian finds an Arabic collection of animal fables whose preface says the stories came from an old Indian book. Going by the chapter, in what language and of what age should she expect that original to be?
o: Sanskrit, and at least 2,200 years old
Sanskrit, but no more than 200 years old
Arabic, and at least 2,200 years old
Tamil, and at least 7,000 years old
questions.a: The chapter says the Panchatantra's original text is in Sanskrit and is at least 2,200 years old, and that its stories travelled to the Arab world. 200 is the estimated number of adaptations, not an age; Arabic is a language the stories travelled into, not the original; and 7,000 is the number of pages the two epics might fill, not anyone's age.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The stories of the Panchatantra have been adapted in almost every Indian language.
Reason (R): The two epics together might fill some 7,000 pages in their original versions.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The chapter says the Panchatantra's stories were adapted in almost every Indian language, and it says the two epics might fill some 7,000 pages; but the length of the epics is a fact about other texts and has nothing to do with how the Panchatantra spread.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
A library in Kolkata has a shelf of six books linked to the Panchatantra:
Book 1: the text in its original language
Book 2: a Bengali retelling
Book 3: a Tamil retelling
Book 4: an Arabic collection inspired by it
Book 5: a French collection inspired by it
Book 6: a collection from Thailand, in Southeast Asia, inspired by it
The catalogue card says: 'Original text: about 500 years old.' The library's rule is that a shelf label must describe every book on the shelf.
(a) In which language is Book 1 written?
(b) Correct the catalogue card, and say by at least how many years it understates the original's age.
(c) Three labels are proposed: X 'The Panchatantra across India', Y 'The Panchatantra beyond India', Z 'One collection becomes many'. Which label meets the library's rule? Justify by saying which books each of the other two leaves out.
questions.a: (a) Sanskrit. (b) The original text is at least 2,200 years old, so the card understates its age by at least 2,200 - 500 = 1,700 years. (c) Label Z. X fits the original and the two Indian retellings (Books 1 to 3) but leaves out the three collections from abroad (Books 4 to 6). Y fits Books 4 to 6 but leaves out the Sanskrit original and the Bengali and Tamil retellings (Books 1 to 3). Z covers the one original and the many retellings and new collections it became, which is how the chapter describes the Panchatantra.
s: Part (a): Sanskrit
Part (b): at least 2,200 years, understated by at least 1,700 years
Part (c): Z, since X leaves out Books 4 to 6 and Y leaves out Books 1 to 3

questions.q: A class is making a poster titled 'One becomes many'. Which fact about the Panchatantra belongs on it?
questions.a: About 200 adaptations exist in more than 50 languages, which the chapter says illustrates how 'one' collection of stories has become 'many'. The Sanskrit original, the animal characters and the life skills are true, but each describes the single collection, not its becoming many.
o: About 200 adaptations exist in more than 50 languages
The original text was composed in the Sanskrit language
Its main characters are animals rather than human heroes
Its stories teach readers important skills for life

questions.q: Dev claims: 'The Panchatantra is an ancient Sanskrit epic about great heroes, and about 200 adaptations of it exist today.' Test each part of his claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. Correct: the original text is in Sanskrit and at least 2,200 years old, and about 200 adaptations exist in more than 50 languages. Wrong: it is not an epic about heroes but a collection of delightful stories with animals as the main characters, teaching life skills; the epics are the Ramayana and the Mahabharata.
s: Sanskrit and ancient (at least 2,200 years): supported
About 200 adaptations: supported
Not an epic about heroes but animal stories teaching life skills; verdict partly right

questions.q: (a) A publisher brings out a Kannada retelling of the Panchatantra and, a year later, a Kannada comic-book version of the same stories. How many adaptations do the two books make, and in how many languages? (b) Use (a) to explain how the chapter can estimate about 200 adaptations but only a little more than 50 languages.
questions.a: (a) 2 adaptations, in 1 language. (b) Several adaptations can be made in the same language, so the count of adaptations can be far larger than the count of languages: about 200 adaptations in more than 50 languages.
s: Part (a): 2 adaptations, 1 language
Part (b): many adaptations can share one language, so adaptations outnumber languages

questions.q: A quiz card reads: 'The Panchatantra's stories never left India.' Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says the stories travelled well beyond India, to Southeast Asia, the Arab world and Europe, inspiring new collections on the way. The other three each leave out or deny part of that: the Arab world was reached, the European versions were not only in Sanskrit, and new collections did arise.
o: They reached Southeast Asia, the Arab world and Europe
They reached Southeast Asia, but never the Arab world
They reached Europe, though only in their Sanskrit form
They reached the Arab world, but no new collections arose

questions.q: Compare the Panchatantra with India's two epics as examples of 'one becoming many'. Then analyse why the chapter calls the epics, not the Panchatantra, 'the most striking case', using what it says about each.
questions.a: Panchatantra: a Sanskrit collection of animal stories teaching life skills, at least 2,200 years old, adapted in almost every Indian language and abroad, about 200 adaptations in more than 50 languages. Epics: two Sanskrit epics of some 7,000 pages about heroes who fight to re-establish dharma, translated or adapted into regional literatures for more than two millenniums, with countless folk versions, about a hundred Mahabharata folk versions in Tamil Nadu alone. Why more striking: beyond translations, many communities, especially tribal ones such as the Bhils, Gonds and Mundas, have their own versions and legends tying their own history and region to the heroes, so that, as K.S. Singh observed, there is hardly a place the heroes did not visit; the epics created a dense web of cultural interactions across India and Asia.
s: Panchatantra: Sanskrit animal stories, about 200 adaptations in 50+ languages
Epics: Sanskrit hero stories, translated and adapted for two millenniums
Countless folk versions, about a hundred in Tamil Nadu alone
Communities and tribes link their own history and region to the heroes
Conclusion: a dense web of interactions makes the epics the most striking case

questions.q: If the number of Panchatantra adaptations estimated in the chapter were shared equally among exactly 50 languages, each language would have ___ adaptations.
Which other example in the chapter grew from 'one' into 'many' in the same way as the Panchatantra, by being retold in other languages?
o: The epics, translated into regional literatures
Makara Sankranti, known by many different regional names
The sari, made in many weaves, designs and colours
Staple grains, combined into thousands of dishes
questions.a: The two epics have been translated or adapted into regional literatures in India and beyond for more than two millenniums: retellings in other languages, like the Panchatantra's adaptations. The festival's many names, the sari's many varieties and the many dishes made from shared grains are other kinds of 'many', not retellings in other languages.

questions.q: A teacher plans two lessons. For Lesson 1 she wants stories in which animals are the main characters and teach life skills; for Lesson 2, stories of heroes who fight to re-establish dharma. (a) Which text from the chapter suits each lesson? (b) Give two things the chapter says the two kinds of text have in common.
questions.a: (a) Lesson 1: the Panchatantra. Lesson 2: the Ramayana or the Mahabharata. (b) Any two: both were first composed in Sanskrit; both have been adapted or translated into many Indian languages and regional literatures; both travelled beyond India; the chapter uses both to show unity in diversity in literature.
