s: Part (a): Panchatantra for Lesson 1, an epic for Lesson 2
Part (b): two shared features, such as Sanskrit originals and wide adaptation

questions.q: A website says the Panchatantra was first written in the 17th century, at the same time chintz was popular in Europe. Show, using the chapter, that this is impossible.
questions.a: The chapter says the original Sanskrit text is at least 2,200 years old. Counting back from 2026 with no year zero, it was composed by 175 BCE at the latest. The 17th century CE (1601-1700) is more than 1,700 years after that, so the text already existed long before the 17th century.
s: At least 2,200 years old, from the chapter
Composed by 175 BCE at the latest
The 17th century CE is far later, so the claim is impossible

questions.q:
A publisher in Hyderabad already sells Panchatantra retellings in Telugu, Hindi, Urdu and English. For next year it has Rs 2,50,000 and two plans.
Plan A: new retellings in Kannada and Marathi, Rs 1,15,000 each.
Plan B: new editions in Arabic and French, Rs 1,30,000 each.
The owner will carry out only a plan that can be paid for in full.
(a) Work out the cost of each plan. Which one fits within the budget?
(b) Which part of the Panchatantra's story, as the chapter tells it, would each plan continue?
(c) In how many languages would the publisher sell the stories after carrying out the plan it can afford?
(d) Plan B's supporters say taking the stories abroad is the bolder continuation. Should the owner choose Plan B anyway? Justify using (a) and (b).
questions.a: (a) Plan A: 2 x 1,15,000 = Rs 2,30,000, which fits, leaving Rs 20,000. Plan B: 2 x 1,30,000 = Rs 2,60,000, which is Rs 10,000 over the budget. (b) Plan A continues the adaptation of the stories in almost every Indian language; Plan B continues their travels to the Arab world and Europe. (c) 4 + 2 = 6 languages. (d) No. Both plans continue a real part of the story the chapter tells, so the chapter gives neither a stronger claim; but Plan B cannot be paid for in full, which breaks the owner's rule, while Plan A fits the budget and still carries the stories into two more Indian languages.
s: Part (a): Plan A Rs 2,30,000 fits; Plan B Rs 2,60,000 is Rs 10,000 over
Part (b): A continues adaptation in Indian languages, B the travels abroad
Part (c): 6 languages
Part (d): no, both fit the chapter's story but only Plan A can be paid for in full

questions.q: How does the Panchatantra differ from the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, as the chapter describes them?
questions.a: The Panchatantra's main characters are animals, while the epics narrate the stories of heroes who fight to re-establish dharma. All three were composed in Sanskrit, the Panchatantra did travel beyond India, and it has been adapted in almost every Indian language, so the other options are wrong.
o: Its main characters are animals, not heroes
It was composed in Sanskrit, while the epics were not
It never travelled outside India, while the epics did
It has no versions in other Indian languages at all

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Panchatantra.
1. Its original text is in Sanskrit.
2. The chapter estimates that about 50 adaptations of it exist in more than 200 languages.
3. Its main characters are heroes who fight to re-establish dharma.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 swaps the figures: about 200 adaptations in more than 50 languages. Statement 3 describes the two epics; the Panchatantra's main characters are animals.
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: Mira asks: 'If the Panchatantra travelled as far as Europe, why use it to show India's unity?' Give two reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Its stories have been adapted in almost every Indian language, so readers across India's many languages share the same stories: unity across linguistic diversity. And the chapter uses it to show that Indian literatures, though extremely diverse, share important themes and concerns, one collection becoming many.
s: Adapted in almost every Indian language, shared across India's languages
Shows diverse Indian literatures sharing themes: one becoming many

questions.q: Asha says: 'The Panchatantra shows unity, because the same stories are found in almost every Indian language.' Bilal replies: 'No, it shows diversity, because there are about 200 different adaptations in more than 50 languages.' Using the chapter, decide who is right and explain.
questions.a: Each has half of it, and the chapter needs both halves. Asha's point is the unity: the same stories and themes are shared across India's languages. Bilal's point is the diversity: about 200 adaptations in more than 50 languages, with new collections inspired abroad. The chapter calls this 'one' collection becoming 'many' and offers it as an illustration of unity in diversity: diverse literatures sharing important themes. So neither is right alone.
s: Asha's half: the same stories shared across languages is the unity
Bilal's half: many adaptations in many languages is the diversity
Judgement: both halves together, one becoming many, unity in diversity

questions.q: Four lines about Indian literatures are proposed for a school magazine. Which one goes beyond what the chapter says?
questions.a: The chapter never says Indian literatures are written in one script; it says they are extremely diverse, among the most abundant in the world, and that despite differences in language and technique they have shared important themes and concerns over centuries.
o: All Indian literatures are written in one shared script
Indian literatures are extremely diverse in their forms
Indian literatures are among the most abundant in the world
Over centuries they have shared important themes and concerns

questions.q:
A museum curator has five books and must label each (A) 'the one', (B) 'one of the many', or (C) 'not linked to the Panchatantra', going by the chapter. Label each book with a reason, then say which books in group (B) show more than a retelling.
Book 1: the stories in their original Sanskrit text
Book 2: a Marathi retelling of the same animal stories
Book 3: an Arabic collection of new stories inspired by them
Book 4: a long poem about heroes who fight to re-establish dharma
Book 5: a collection from Southeast Asia inspired by them
questions.a: Book 1 is (A): the original Sanskrit collection, the 'one'. Book 2 is (B): an adaptation in an Indian language, and the chapter says the stories were adapted in almost every Indian language. Books 3 and 5 are (B): the stories travelled to the Arab world and to Southeast Asia. Book 4 is (C): heroes fighting to re-establish dharma describes the epics, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, whereas the Panchatantra's main characters are animals. Books 3 and 5 show more than a retelling: the chapter says that on their travels the stories inspired new collections of stories.
s: Book 1 as the one, the Sanskrit original
Book 2 as one of the many, adapted in an Indian language
Books 3 and 5 as the many beyond India
Book 4 not linked: hero and dharma stories are the epics
Books 3 and 5 inspired new collections, more than retelling

questions.q:
Match each claim about the epics in Column A with the evidence the chapter gives for it in Column B.
Column A: 1. The epics were known even to people who could not read  2. Folk versions are plentiful even within one State  3. A community marks a hero's passing through its own land  4. The epics spread beyond the borders of India
Column B: a. The Irula shrine to the Pandavas in the Nilgiris  b. Villagers whom Nehru met knowing hundreds of verses by heart  c. Translations and adaptations into literatures in India and beyond  d. About a hundred Mahabharata folk versions counted in Tamil Nadu
questions.a: 1-b (Nehru found illiterate villagers knowing hundreds of verses), 2-d (about a hundred folk versions in Tamil Nadu alone), 3-a (the Irula shrine commemorating the Pandavas' passing), 4-c (translated or adapted into regional literatures in India and beyond for more than two millenniums).

questions.q: A student thinks tribal versions of the epics belong only to the three tribes the chapter names first: the Bhils, the Gonds and the Mundas. Which detail in the chapter corrects her?
o: Most northeast and Himalayan tribes have versions too
Tribal versions exist only in written Sanskrit form
Tamil Nadu's survey counted versions in just three tribes
Only the Irula keep any legend of the Pandavas at all
questions.a: The chapter names 'the Bhils, the Gonds, the Mundas and many more', and adds that most tribes of India's northeast and Himalayan regions, including Kashmir, have had their own version of one or both epics. Tribal adaptations are transmitted orally, not in written Sanskrit; the Tamil Nadu survey counted about a hundred folk versions, not tribes; and the Irula shrine is one example, not the only legend.

questions.q: Riya claims: 'Only people who can read Sanskrit really know the Ramayana and the Mahabharata.' Test her claim against the chapter and give your verdict.
questions.a: No. For more than two millenniums the epics have been translated or adapted into regional literatures, and there are countless folk versions, including tribal versions passed on orally. Nehru found that in popular translations and paraphrases the epics were widely known among the masses, and illiterate villagers knew hundreds of verses by heart. So the epics are known far beyond Sanskrit readers.
s: Translated and adapted into regional literatures, with countless folk and oral versions
Nehru: illiterate villagers knew hundreds of verses
Verdict: No, the epics are known well beyond Sanskrit readers

questions.q: A tribal community's oral legend says that Draupadi once rested beside the river in its valley. Which observation in the chapter does this legend fit best?
questions.a: The chapter says tribal adaptations are passed on orally along with legends on how the heroes of the epics, generally the Pandavas or Draupadi, visited the tribes' own regions. The page count, Nehru's villagers knowing verses and the Tamil Nadu count of folk versions are true, but none of them is about heroes visiting a community's own land.
o: Legends tell of heroes visiting a tribe's own region
The two epics together fill some 7,000 pages in Sanskrit
Villagers knew hundreds of verses of the epics by heart
About a hundred folk versions were counted in Tamil Nadu

questions.q: True or False? 'In the tribal legends the chapter describes, only the heroes of the epics, never their rivals, are said to have visited the tribe's region.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. The visitors are generally any or all of the five Pandavas and their wife Draupadi, but sometimes also their cousin and adversary Duryodhana.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: sometimes their rival cousin Duryodhana is also said to have visited

questions.q:
A Class 6 team spent a month recording stories told by elders in their district and made this tally:
Mahabharata folk tales: 12
Ramayana folk tales: 9
Legends of a Pandava visiting a hill near the village: 4
Legend of Duryodhana camping by the river: 1
The team's report may carry one concluding sentence, and it must not claim more than the tally and the chapter support.
(a) How many items in the tally are linked to the Mahabharata?
(b) Which entries match the legends the chapter describes among tribal communities, and which of them names a figure the chapter says appears in such legends only 'sometimes'?
(c) Sentence X: 'Like the communities in the chapter, our district keeps legends that tie the epic heroes to its own land.' Sentence Y: 'Our district has nearly twice as many Mahabharata items as Ramayana ones, so the Mahabharata matters more to India than the Ramayana.' Which should the report carry? Justify.
questions.a: (a) 12 + 4 + 1 = 17. (b) The legends of a Pandava visiting the hill and of Duryodhana camping by the river; Duryodhana is the one the chapter says appears only sometimes (the visitors are generally the Pandavas or Draupadi). (c) Sentence X. Sentence Y starts from a true local figure (17 against 9 is nearly twice), but one district cannot speak for all of India, and the chapter says that what K.S. Singh observed of the Mahabharata may be said of the Ramayana too. Sentence X rests on the 5 local legends and matches the chapter's account of communities preserving legends that connect their own history with the epics.
s: Part (b): the hill and river legends; Duryodhana appears only sometimes
Part (c): Sentence X, since one district cannot speak for India and the chapter treats both epics alike

questions.q: A student writes: 'Tribal versions of the epics were copied from written Sanskrit books.' Which fact in the chapter goes against her?
questions.a: The chapter says tribal adaptations are transmitted orally. The other three are true facts from the chapter, but none of them says how tribal versions are passed on, so none contradicts her.
o: Tribal adaptations of the epics are transmitted orally
The epics were translated into regional literatures
The two epics together fill some 7,000 pages
A scholar counted about a hundred versions in Tamil Nadu

questions.q: (a) A student writes: 'In the Mahabharata, the Pandavas, helped by Hanuman, defeat a demon who had kidnapped their wife.' Which epic's story has she mixed into her sentence? (b) Rewrite the sentence so that it matches the chapter's account of the Mahabharata.
questions.a: (a) The Ramayana: there Rama, helped by Lakshmana and Hanuman, defeats the demon Ravana, who had kidnapped his wife Sita. (b) In the Mahabharata, the Pandavas, with Krishna's help, fight their own cousins, the Kauravas, to recover their kingdom.
s: Part (a): the Ramayana's story has been mixed in
Part (b): the Pandavas, helped by Krishna, fight their cousins the Kauravas to recover their kingdom

questions.q: Taking the chapter's round figure for the length of the two epics together in their original versions, a scholar reading 25 pages a day would need about ___ days to read both.
A summary for a class wall reads: 'In the Ramayana, Rama, helped by his cousin Lakshmana and by Krishna, defeats Ravana.' Which correction makes it match the chapter?
questions.a: Lakshmana is Rama's brother, and Rama is helped by Hanuman; Krishna helps the Pandavas in the Mahabharata. Lakshmana is not Rama's son, Krishna does not help the Kauravas, and Rama's enemy is Ravana, not Duryodhana.
o: Lakshmana is his brother; Hanuman, not Krishna, helps
Lakshmana is his son, and Hanuman, not Krishna, helps him
Lakshmana is right, but Krishna helps the Kauravas instead
Rama defeats Duryodhana, the rival cousin, not Ravana

questions.q:
Read this extract from Jawaharlal Nehru, given in the chapter:
'The old epics of India, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata and other books, in popular translations and paraphrases, were widely known among the masses ... Illiterate villagers would know hundreds of verses by heart and their conversation would be full of references to them ...'
(a) When, and on what kind of journey, did Nehru make this observation?
(b) Give two pieces of evidence from the chapter, NOT found in this extract, that the epics are known widely across India.
(c) Explain how Nehru's observation and your evidence together support the chapter's theme of unity in diversity.
questions.a: (a) Before Independence, when he travelled to many parts of India. (b) Any two: for more than two millenniums the epics have been translated or adapted into regional literatures; a survey in Tamil Nadu alone counted about a hundred folk versions of the Mahabharata; tribal communities such as the Bhils, Gonds and Mundas, and most tribes of the northeast and Himalayan regions, have their own versions; the Irula keep a shrine to the Pandavas' passing; K.S. Singh observed that, according to folklore, there is hardly a place the heroes did not visit. questions.q:
A tourism board is planning an all-India campaign based on the epics. It wants every State to see itself in the campaign without claiming more than its sources. It has two draft slogans.
Slogan X: 'Walk where legend says the Pandavas walked: almost everywhere in India.'
Slogan Y: 'Visit five places where legend says the Pandavas stayed.'
Its researchers found this statement by an anthropologist: 'There is hardly a place in the country which the epic heroes such as the Pandavas, did not visit according to folklores.'
(a) Which words of the statement show that it rests on folklore rather than on records, and why should a slogan keep that point?
(b) Give one example from the chapter of a community that marks the Pandavas' passing through its own area.
(c) Which slogan should the board choose? Justify using (a), (b) and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 'according to folklores'; a slogan that dropped it would present a legend as a fact. (b) The Irula tribals, who maintain the Pancha Pandavar shrine in a forest of the Nilgiris, Tamil Nadu, to commemorate the Pandavas' passing through the area. (c) Slogan X. Slogan Y is accurate and concrete (the Irula shrine would be one such place), but five places would leave most States out of an all-India campaign. Slogan X keeps the word 'legend', as K.S. Singh keeps 'according to folklores', and his remark, with the many communities that link the heroes to their own regions, supports 'almost everywhere'.
s: Part (a): 'according to folklores'; keep it so legend is not sold as fact
Part (b): the Irula shrine in the Nilgiris
Part (c): Slogan X, since it matches Singh's folklore remark and suits all-India, while five places leave most States out

questions.q: Compare the two ways the chapter says the epics spread: through translations into regional literatures, and through folk and tribal versions. Then analyse which of the two shows more clearly that communities made the epics their own.
questions.a: Literary spread: the two Sanskrit epics, some 7,000 pages together, have been translated or adapted into regional literatures in India and beyond for more than two millenniums. Folk and tribal spread: there are countless folk versions, about a hundred Mahabharata versions in Tamil Nadu alone; tribal communities such as the Bhils, Gonds and Mundas, and most tribes of the northeast and Himalayan regions including Kashmir, have their own versions, passed on orally. Analysis: the folk and tribal versions show it more clearly, because communities preserved legends connecting their own history with the epics, saying the Pandavas, Draupadi or even Duryodhana visited their region, and the Irula keep a shrine to the Pandavas' passing.
s: Literary spread: translated and adapted into regional literatures for two millenniums
Folk spread: countless versions, about a hundred in Tamil Nadu
Tribal versions passed on orally, with named tribes
Legends linking a community's own history and region to the heroes
Judgement: folk and tribal versions show communities making the epics their own
